newsitem.title: USA: Nebraska tour sees above-average corn yields.
newsitem.headline: Nebraska tour sees above-average corn yields.

text.p: The first leg of a corn tour through Nebraska ended Tuesday with participants saying the average potential yield was running well above the historical average yield for the seven counties visited.

Using a standardized formula developed at the University of Illinois, tour members calculated an average potential corn yield for the first day of 170.2 bushels per acre (bpa), with a range of 133 to 237.5 bpa.

The figure of 170.2 bpa compared to the Nebraska Department of Agricultural Statistics' most recent statewide estimated corn yield of 152.7 bpa. The five-year average yield for the seven counties was 135 bpa.

This was the first time the Nebraska Corn Board has undertaken such a tour, which meant participants could not draw comparisons with data from previous years -- a practice that is common on most U.S. crop tours.

But Randy Klein, director of market development for the Nebraska Corn Board, warned against becoming too optimistic over Tuesday's yield number. He noted that the tour only took samples in nine irrigated fields -- a less-than-accurate representation of the true yield outlook for dryland and irrigated fields across the whole state.

"It is an average of 18 samples in nine fields, and it can't be equated to a state average," Klein said. "We also have to keep in mind that we were in some of the leading producing counties and visiting some of the top producers in the state."
Tour vehicles travelled along a single route through southern Nebraska and made scheduled stops with producers in Seward, Saline, Fillmore, Clay, Adams, Kearney and Phelps counties.
Approximately a dozen people took part on the tour's first day, including agriculture statisticians, crop analysts and other members of the grain industry.
Most producers who were interviewed Tuesday said they were looking at harvesting one of the best crops in the past five years.
Participants saw little evidence of disease or insect pressure. But they noted that a cool, late growing season had led to lower-than-normal test weights and higher-than-normal moisture levels.
The tour found test weights were running on average around 55 pounds. Most moisture levels were between 25 and 28 percent.
"It just isn't drying down like we want it to because we just haven't had the heat units," said Ron Ochsner, a producer in Clay County.

Nebraska ranks as the third largest corn producing state, supplying approximately 13 percent of the U.S. corn crop after Iowa and Illinois. In 1995, Nebraska produced 854.7 billion bushels, with a yield of 111 bpa.
The tour was set to conclude Thursday in Lincoln, Nebraska.
